power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The number of study participants will be 20 -30 and will be recruited using purposive sampling method with the number of participants determined by data saturation, the point at which no new themes emerge from the interviews [38] and with regard to balanced representation across population groups. This target is based on the information power; that is, the richer the information of the sample, the fewer number of participants [39]. The sample will be purposefully selected from a range of key and vulnerable groups including sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender and hijra people, people who inject drugs (PWID), migrant people, and partners of key population members, further differentiated by gender, hijra/transgender identity, migration history, marital status, time since diagnosis, and duration of ART to capture varied lived experience along the HIV care pathway. The findings of this modest sample are supported by five features: a narrow aim, a well-defined population (young people living with HIV age 18 to 30), in-depth dialogic interviews, and a case-focused thematic framework analysis [39], and analysis based on existing theory (emerging adulthood and HIV-stigma frameworks). This range is supported by empirical findings, which indicate that thematic saturation is usually reached after 12 interviews in a focused purposive sample [38], and code saturation is typically achieved after nine and meaning saturation is usually reached after 16-24 interviews [40]. 20-30 is a sample size above both thresholds and allows for the planned key-population versus general-population comparison, while other studies of YLWH have been published with 10-20 participants [21, 41].

text.text: Bangladesh is a country with low HIV prevalence, but case detection has more than doubled in 2020-24, reaching 1,891 cases in the most recently reported year, and the number of cases is growing in the 18-24 age group.

There is little qualitative evidence that describes the journey from suspected exposure to diagnosis for young people in Bangladesh, and no comparative evidence of this journey between keypopulation and general-population youth.

To explore the pathway to HIV testing and diagnosis, what motivated testing, and the life outlook of people living with HIV in Bangladesh aged 18-30 years, and to compare these between key-population and general-population participants.
This qualitative exploratory study uses semi-structured in-depth interviews, guided by the theory of emerging adulthood and the HIV Stigma Framework.

Purposive maximum-variation sampling (20-30 participants) will recruit people aged 18-30, diagnosed within that age range and currently on antiretroviral therapy, balanced between key and general populations.
Participants will be recruited through Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and Ashar Alo Society, Dhaka, and interviewed privately in Bangla.
Recordings will be transcribed, translated into English, and analysed with the Framework Method in MAXQDA, with saturation judged within each group.

text.text: It happens in a specific social and legal environment: in a Muslim dominated society marriage is sometimes a social arrangement and/or is expected and hijra identity is formally recognised, though homosexual behaviour is criminalised, resulting in some young people being visible and vulnerable.

After diagnosis, PLHIV in Bangladesh continue to experience stigma from society, side effects of medication, financial problems, long distances to ART centres and lack of support from family members [18], internalised stigma around living with HIV [19], and limited uptake of testing, with many people being diagnosed late, often incidentally [16].

text.text: There is strong evidence available on prevalence, surveillance, key-population programming, ART uptake and discrete service barriers, but relatively less evidence on the experiences of young people in Bangladesh themselves around experiencing a transition from suspected exposure to a life remade around HIV.

Some of what this silence might be hiding is suggested by international evidence: qualitative research in sub-Saharan Africa indicates that there is substantial initial psychological trauma and deep internalised stigma after diagnosis; that specialised counselling helps adolescents transition from suicidal thinking to selfacceptance [20]; that consent rules and poor confidentiality contribute to low uptake of services and disengagement from health clinics, particularly youth, who are targeted by informal community workers [21, 22]; and Kenyan evidence demonstrating that difficulty with disclosure is directly linked to disengagement from services [23].

text.text: Very little of this evidence is from Bangladesh, few studies focus on the age band of 18-30 years, and even fewer consider the process from exposure to diagnosis as one continuous time series.

Importantly, no qualitative study has been conducted to date in Bangladesh comparing the pathway and the resulting life perspective of key-population younger youth to generalpopulation younger youth, as done in this study.

A qualitative study is thus needed and appropriate for this gap; the question of "why" is raised, the process of referral is described, the emotional and social uptake of diagnosis is explored and the future imaginings of the young are discussed.

This study has the potential to uncover triggers to test, missed prevention opportunities, real-world referral pathways through HIV services, and post-diagnostic experiences of hope, fear, acceptance and planning for the future; it can also determine if participants believe HIV is incurable, curable, or manageable like other chronic illnesses such as diabetes, or whether greater awareness of HIV prior to exposure could have influenced behavior.

Peer-led programmes elsewhere, such as Community Adolescent Treatment Supporters in Zimbabwe, have helped young people to rebuild their hope and to stay in care [25], and meaningful youth involvement in the design of services in Kenya has led to optimisation of testing, linkage and retention [26], so for young PLHIV in Bangladesh, the question is whether such supports are sufficient.

text.text: • How do young people living with HIV, aged 18-30 years in Bangladesh, experience the journey from suspected exposure to HIV diagnosis, what motivated them to test, and what is their current outlook on life?
• What events, risk perceptions, or personal experiences led participants to HIV testing and diagnosis?
• How were participants referred to HIV testing, counselling, ART, and related services through health facilities, NGOs, or community networks?
• How do participants describe their current outlook on life after diagnosis, including hope, fear, acceptance, uncertainty, and future planning?
• How do participants perceive HIV, such as curable, fatal, or manageable like other chronic conditions such as diabetes mellitus?
• What awareness and perceptions of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) did participants hold prior to diagnosis?
• How, if at all, do the exposure-to-diagnosis journey and current outlook on life differ between key-population and non-key/general-population participants?

The age group 18-30 was selected intentionally, and is different from the 15-24 age group that is used for reporting HIV internationally, for four reasons.
For one thing, the 15-24 is not a Bangladeshi policy or legal category.

United Nations and UNAIDS have defined the youth age range as 15-24 years for reporting purpose, while the age range of youth has been defined as 18-35 years in Bangladesh's National Youth Policy 2017, and 15-29 years in the Commonwealth of Australia's definition. [32] .

text.text: The selected band is thus entirely included in the national definition of youth and it starts from the point where the national definition of youth starts.
Second, in terms of age, 18 years is the age of maturity in Bangladesh.

The Majority Act, 1875 specifies that a person who is domiciled in Bangladesh turns major at 18 years and not earlier. [33] For minors, Bangladesh Medical Research Council guidelines call for consent to be obtained from parent/legal guardian and assent to be obtained based on the child's capacity [34].

text.text: Setting the lower age limit at 18 will allow all participants in an HIV study to consent independently and confidentially, whereas guardian consent would force disclosure of HIV status to family members, which is itself a known harm and a significant disincentive to participation.
Third, there is a maximum limit of 30, based on developmental theory.

The transition between adolescence and full adulthood (18-29 years) is a unique developmental phase, according to Arnett's theory of emerging adulthood, where there is identity exploration, instability in place, selffocus, a sense of "in-betweenness", and a feeling of possibilities.
In this phase, majority of people delay marriage and parenthood till about 30 and use their twenties to try out relationship and career.

These are the very processes that contribute to HIV exposure and the meaning a young person attributes to a diagnosis: sexual debut, partner formation, migration for study or work, and entering into marriage.

A ceiling of 30 (instead of 24) thus includes university students, migrant and early career workers, and newly married people who would otherwise be among the "missing" or cut off by the 15-24 age group.
Fourth, the age range of 18-30 has been used previously in HIV studies with emerging adults.

In Zimbabwe, a qualitative study involving emerging adults (18-29 years) living with HIV interviewed them using a semi-structured interview, and found that they have lower adherence to ART and higher viral non-suppression rates compared to older adults. Despite being a low prevalence HIV context, HIV diagnoses in Bangladesh are increasing at a disproportionate rate for young people, and there is little qualitative evidence understanding the pathway of suspected exposure, to diagnosis and beyond.

This study seeks to leverage youth-friendly testing and expand awareness of PrEP, while supporting linkage to ART, challenging stigma, and providing locally generated evidence to inform HIV policy nationally, by understanding the experience of this journey as a lived one and by comparing key-population and general-population experiences.
